title: Dry seasons
hookLine: John of the Cross's dark night and every practitioner's flat months: push harder, or keep one thing quietly?
tomorrow: a cook said his noisy kitchen was as holy as church. how?

lines: A FRIAR IN A LOCKED CELL.
A SOUL OUT ON A DARK NIGHT.
cards: A playlist that lifted you for months suddenly does nothing. Same songs. No lift.
Practice can go like that too. A Spanish friar, John of the Cross, was locked in a small cell by members of his own religious order who opposed his reforms.
He escaped, and later wrote a poem about a soul slipping out of a quiet house on a dark night. Then he wrote a whole book explaining that darkness.

teach.h: A DRYNESS WHERE PRAYER GOES FLAT.
teach.b: So was the dark a sign to quit? In The Dark Night, John describes a dryness where prayer that used to feel sweet goes flat. His view: this can be God at work, weaning a person off the need for good feelings.
His counsel is to stop straining for the old sweetness, stay quietly, with simple loving attention, and keep going. Now the other view, and it has a real case.
Some spiritual directors in John's day said: if prayer has gone flat, work harder. Go back to the meditations that used to work. Push.
And John himself grants part of it. Dryness, he says, can come from slackness, or from a low mood or a sick body, and then it's no holy night at all.
So he gives signs to tell them apart: one is that you still care, and worry that you're failing. Where the two views part is what to do next.

teach.h: THE DIRECTORS: PUSH THE OLD METHOD.
teach.b: The directors say force the old method.

teach.h: SIGNS TO TELL DRYNESS FROM DRIFT.
teach.b: John says forcing it only frets the soul. Neither says quit. That's John's counsel, which Christian contemplatives still turn to: don't force the old feeling, don't walk away.
Keep one thing. And if the flatness spreads to all of life, a doctor belongs in the picture too.

how: In the Christian contemplative tradition, John of the Cross's Dark Night describes dry stretches in prayer; his counsel is to keep praying simply and quietly rather than force old methods. Spiritual directors still use his signs to tell dryness from drift.

o: flat stretches in practice, kept with one small thing
a time when you should stop practicing for a while
the months of the year when it barely rains at all

games.q: the dark night: tap the pairs.
p: wrote a book explaining the dark night
prayer that used to feel sweet goes flat
push harder, go back to the old method

s: John said every dry stretch is a holy dark night
he said dryness can also come from slackness, low mood or illness, and gave signs to tell them apart.
John's counsel was to stop straining for the old sweetness
stay quietly, with simple loving attention, and keep going.
a dry season means the practice has failed and should end
neither John nor the directors said quit. they argued about how to keep going.

games.q: your friend says: when prayer goes flat, push harder and go back to what used to work. what's the best case for her view?
o: sometimes flatness really is drift, and steady effort brings you back.
good feelings are the whole point of prayer, so chase them.
if prayer feels flat, God has stopped listening.
games.why: John himself agreed dryness can come from slackness. he just held that, when it's the dark night, forcing the old method only frets the soul.

practice: Choose the one small piece of your practice you'd keep through a dry season: one line, one breath, one minute. Say it out loud once. Then sit for the rest of the time with no feeling expected, just keeping it.

wordCard.voice: Dry seasons: stretches when practice feels like nothing, what John of the Cross called a dark night, kept with one small thing.

carryVoice: Your line: keep one thing. John's counsel in the dark was not more force, and not leaving. See you tomorrow.
